## Proof

Let $X$ be the **Cantor set** $C \subset [0,1]$, equipped with the subspace metric inherited from $\mathbb{R}$.

**$X$ is a compact metric space with $|X|>1$.**

The Cantor set is a closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$, hence compact by the Heine–Borel theorem. As a subspace of $\mathbb{R}$ it is a metric space. It is uncountable (e.g. it is in bijection with $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ via ternary expansions), so in particular $|X|>1$.

**A useful representation of $C$.**

Recall the standard homeomorphism
$$\varphi : \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} \longrightarrow C, \qquad \varphi\big((a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots)\big) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{2a_n}{3^n},$$
where $\{0,1\}$ carries the discrete topology and $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ the product topology. This map is well-defined, continuous, bijective, and since $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ is compact (Tychonoff / countable product of compact spaces) and $C$ is Hausdorff, $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism. Thus
$$C \;\cong\; \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}.$$

**$C \times C \cong C$.**

Using the representation above,
$$C \times C \;\cong\; \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} \times \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}.$$

Now $\mathbb{N} \sqcup \mathbb{N}$ (the disjoint union of two copies of $\mathbb{N}$) is in bijection with $\mathbb{N}$; explicitly, the map
$$\Phi : \mathbb{N} \sqcup \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}, \qquad \Phi(n,0)=2n-1,\quad \Phi(n,1)=2n$$
is a bijection. This bijection induces, for each $i\in\{0,1\}$, a coordinate-shuffling homeomorphism
$$\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} \times \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} \;\longrightarrow\; \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}\sqcup\mathbb{N}} \;\longrightarrow\; \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}},$$
given concretely by
$$\big((a_1,a_2,\dots),\,(b_1,b_2,\dots)\big) \;\longmapsto\; (a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2,a_3,b_3,\dots).$$

This is a homeomorphism (it is a bijection, and it is continuous with continuous inverse because it merely permutes coordinates, and the product topology is preserved under reindexing by any bijection of the index set). Therefore
$$C \times C \;\cong\; \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} \times \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} \;\cong\; \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} \;\cong\; C.$$

**Conclusion.**

The Cantor set $C$ is a compact metric space with $|C|>1$, and $C \times C$ is homeomorphic to $C$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
